findings.title: Shell or file writes run without a pause
findings.short: 2 rules and 1 setting approve without asking
findings.lead: Your settings approve shell commands or file writes without asking, or skip the approval prompt. Judgment moves from the risky step to reading diffs after the fact.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

evidence.metric: Bash: blanket shell allow
Write: blanket write allow
defaultMode: bypassPermissions: bypass or auto-approve default mode

why: Found: Bash, Write and defaultMode: bypassPermissions.
Each one applies in every project that reads these settings.
problem: A human checkpoint exists in name only, so out-of-scope writes are found by chance.
Approvals that never ask cannot be tuned to the risky steps.

pivot.action: Replace blanket allow rules with scoped ones and set the default permission mode back to ask.
pivot.setup_note: Keep a scoped allow list for the commands you run every day; anything outward-facing or destructive still asks.

benefit.headline: Judgment where it counts
benefit.sub: You decide at the risky step only

benefit.headline: 3 entries to scope
benefit.sub: Each becomes a narrow allow or a prompt

findings.title: Instruction files unchanged for over 180 days
findings.lead: Some instruction or memory files have not changed in over 180 days. The agent still follows them, including any rule that no longer holds.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

evidence.metric: 658 days since last change
658 days since last change

why: 2 of 2 instruction or memory files last changed over 180 days ago.
The oldest last changed 658 days ago.
Dates come from the last git commit, or from the file time when git has no commit for the file.
problem: Stale guidance is trusted guidance, so an outdated rule looks intentional.
A fix you make in chat is lost when the file still says the old thing.

pivot.action: Open the oldest instruction file, delete what no longer holds, and note today as its review date.
pivot.before_scrubbed:
# Project rules
Use the legacy build script for releases.
Pin the old model alias for code review.
pivot.after_scrubbed:
# Project rules
Owner: platform team. Reviewed: (today's date)
Use `make release` for releases.
pivot.setup_note: Set a recurring reminder at your review cadence so the next pass starts from a tripwire, not from drift.

benefit.headline: Rules you can trust
benefit.sub: Each file carries a recent review

findings.title: Always-loaded instructions are 44 KB
findings.lead: Every session loads these instructions before the first prompt. Rules that apply everywhere compete with rules that rarely apply.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

evidence.metric: 44 KB

why: Always-loaded files total 44 KB for the largest project, over the 40 KB line.
The largest single file is 44 KB.
The 40 KB line is this tool's policy, not a SHRINE number.
problem: Context spent on rarely used rules is context not spent on the task.
Long files hide the rules that matter most.

pivot.action: Move rarely used sections out of always-loaded files into skills or files loaded on demand.
pivot.before_scrubbed: CLAUDE.md holds the whole runbook, every past incident, and the style guide, loaded every session.
pivot.after_scrubbed: CLAUDE.md keeps the rules that apply to every task and links to a runbook skill and a style guide file read on demand.
pivot.setup_note: Measure the always-loaded size again after the move; each removed line is context every session no longer pays for.

benefit.headline: 4 KB to move
benefit.sub: To get under the policy line

findings.title: Instruction files have no owner or review date
findings.lead: Some instruction files do not say who owns them or when they were last reviewed. Without an owner, nobody is asked to look again.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

evidence.metric: missing owner and review date
missing owner and review date

why: 2 of 2 instruction files lack an owner line, a review date line, or both.
The format is this tool's convention, for example Owner: and Reviewed: with a date.
problem: Nobody is prompted to review a file that has no owner.
Without a review date, file age is the only signal, and age alone says little.

pivot.action: Add an owner line and a review date line to the top of each instruction file.
pivot.before_scrubbed:
# Project rules
Run the linter before you commit.
pivot.after_scrubbed:
# Project rules
Owner: (your name or team)
Reviewed: (today's date)
Run the linter before you commit.
pivot.setup_note: The owner and review line format is this tool's convention; any consistent format works if it is easy to find.

benefit.headline: Clear ownership
benefit.sub: Someone is asked to look again

shrine_refs.quote: Drift: skills tuned against a retired model still load, and nobody can say who owns them

findings.title: Setup has no hooks, skills or memory
findings.lead: The harness can run checks, load task skills, and keep memory across sessions. Your setup does not use at least one of these from any source, plugins included.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

evidence.metric: no hooks
no skills
no memory

why: Counted from user, project, and plugin sources: 0 hooks, 0 skills, 0 memory files.
This tool's own skill is not counted.
problem: Checks you repeat by hand stay habits instead of gates.
Each session starts from scratch on what the harness could carry.

pivot.action: Add one extension for the gap named here: a hook for a check you repeat, a skill for a task you repeat, or a memory file.
pivot.before_scrubbed: Every session starts from the same chat prompt; the test run is typed by hand after each change.
pivot.after_scrubbed: A post-edit hook runs the tests; a skill holds the release steps; a memory file keeps project facts across sessions.
pivot.setup_note: Start with the check you type most often; a hook turns it from a habit into a gate.

benefit.headline: Checks that run themselves
benefit.sub: A hook replaces a typed command

findings.title: Session history is kept for 30 days
findings.lead: Session history older than the retention window is deleted. Comparing behavior across releases needs history that outlives one cycle.

confidence.label: high
confidence.basis: deterministic fact from your setup files

why: History retention is 30 days, the harness default.
This finding is informational; it changes nothing about how sessions run.
problem: Behavior shifts cannot be compared once older sessions are gone.
Later inspect runs see only the last 30 days.

pivot.action: Raise the history retention setting so past sessions stay on disk long enough to compare.
pivot.before_scrubbed: Session history is cleared after the default window, so last quarter's behavior cannot be compared with today's.
pivot.after_scrubbed: User settings set cleanupPeriodDays to keep 90 days of sessions for comparison.
pivot.setup_note: Retention only affects your own machine; pick a window that covers at least one full release cycle.

findings.lead: In some judged episodes, a rule or limit the agent needed arrived in your second or third message, after it had started. A model judged these, so treat them as leads.
findings.caveat: A model read these episodes. Its accuracy is not yet measured. Treat this as a lead, not a verdict.

confidence.label: medium
confidence.basis: 5 of 12 judged episodes, bar 3; judge agreed on 100% of corrections; accuracy not yet measured

evidence.metric: 5 code-flagged correction candidates across 5 judged episodes
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner you
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner you
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner you
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner you
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner you

why: 5 of 12 judged episodes had a correction in your second or third message that supplied a constraint.
That constraint was in neither your first message nor the instruction files loaded for that session.
Code flags the correction candidates; a model judged whether each one supplied a constraint.
problem: Each late constraint costs a round trip, and the agent redoes work it already did.
A constraint that lives only in chat comes back in later sessions.

pivot.action: Put the constraints you know in the first message: what must not change, the tools to use, and what done looks like.
pivot.before_scrubbed: Add a CSV export to report 0.
pivot.after_scrubbed: Add a CSV export to report 0. Actually, use semicolons as the separator and keep the header row.
pivot.setup_note: A constraint you state twice belongs in an instruction file or a skill, so it arrives first every time.

benefit.sub: Each is listed in the evidence

findings.title: Loaded rules were restated in chat (candidate)
findings.lead: In some judged episodes, you corrected the agent with a rule your loaded instruction files already held. A model judged these, so treat them as leads.
findings.caveat: A model read these episodes. Its accuracy is not yet measured. Treat this as a lead, not a verdict.

confidence.label: medium
confidence.basis: 3 of 12 judged episodes, bar 3; judge agreed on 100% of corrections; accuracy not yet measured

evidence.metric: 3 code-flagged correction candidates across 3 judged episodes
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner model
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner model
judge read: supplies a constraint; owner model

why: 3 of 12 judged episodes had a correction that repeated a rule from a loaded instruction file.
The rule was matched by an exact quote from the instruction text loaded for that session.
Code flags the correction candidates; a model judged whether each one repeated a loaded rule.
problem: A rule the agent does not follow is a rule you enforce by hand.
Restating it in chat fixes one session, not the next.

pivot.action: Turn the rule you restated into a check that runs on its own: a hook or a test that fails when the rule is broken.
pivot.before_scrubbed:
CLAUDE.md: Never edit generated files.
Chat: Do not touch the generated client, I said that already.
pivot.after_scrubbed:
CLAUDE.md: Never edit generated files.
Hook: before an edit, block paths under the generated folder and say why.
pivot.setup_note: When a loaded rule is not followed, enforcement beats repetition: the hook catches the miss before you do.

benefit.headline: 3 corrections a check could catch
benefit.sub: A hook or gate runs the rule for you

benefit.headline: 0 messages after these corrections
benefit.sub: Fewer when the rule is enforced

lines: 66 sessions reviewed, 136 episodes
One project dominates: 98 of 136 episodes (72%) come from 1 of 4 projects, so every rate here mostly describes that project.
1171 human messages, 22 interrupts, 3 compactions
Subagent share of attributable tokens: 45% of 18,400,000 tokens. Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.
Correction candidates: 40 human messages, each counted once however many cues it holds. Count only, not judged.
Identical tool-call retries: 61 of 5200 tool calls (1.2 per 100 tool calls). Count only: polling and re-reads look the same. Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.
Done claims with no test or check run before them: 4 of 12 claims. Count only: the claim pattern is not precise enough for a finding. Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.

Rework (named reverts) within 72 hours: 3 of 6 flagged episodes with linked commits (50%, a small sample under 15 episodes), 10 of 80 other episodes with linked commits (13%). Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.
Rework (named reverts) within 72 hours: 2 of 60 episodes with linked commits (3%). Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.

Possible rework (later-session fix): 7 of 60 episodes with linked commits had a fix commit on the same files from a later session, at least 1 hour after. Candidate count only. Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.
Possible rework (file overlap): 48 of 136 episodes had a changed file touched again within 72 hours. Candidate count only. Mostly 1 project: 72% of episodes.
Iteration commits: 85 fix commits in the same session or within 1 hour. Normal iteration, not rework.
Housekeeping automation left out: 987 of 1172 sessions (84%)
Spawned automation: 100 sessions linked to 14 of your sessions as byproducts, not judged
Unattributed automation: 20 sessions with no parent session found, not read

Dropped before counting: 9 resent messages (the same text sent again after an interrupt or an unanswered send), and 41 copied messages in 3 session files that repeat lines already read (a fork, a resume, or one session saved in 2 folders; 1 of 3 files had nothing new and was left out).
The session driving this run was left out.
12 of 12 sampled episodes judged in 12 model calls, retries included (fixture-model).
Outcomes: 4 resolved, 0 abandoned, 8 reworked, 0 could not tell.
Corrections traced: 8 on code-flagged turns; 0 could not be attributed and are counted only.
Answers rejected: 0 invalid, 0 refusals.
Tokens used: 50,400 tokens on your own account, against an estimate of 52,000 to 74,000 tokens.
